text: Improving an agent through successive revisions requires balancing exploration and evaluation under a limited budget. A narrow search can miss useful sequences of edits, while fully evaluating every intermediate version can exhaust the budget before those sequences yield a verified improvement. We introduce Spec ulative R ecursive S elf- I mprovement ( SpecRSI ), which drafts executable successor agents before their predecessors are fully evaluated, while requiring complete verification before adoption. Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS) allocates the budget between further edits and outstanding checks using the predicted verified return of a continuation. Group Verification Optimization (GVO) learns the improver from completed searches while keeping the real evaluator fixed. In the main scientific comparison, terminal gains exceed Janus by 33.3%–40.0%. Additional evaluations show that SpecRSI outperforms Janus in all 50 scientific backbone–task pairs and exceeds MetaRSI-v1 by 1.85%–2.38% in macro-average system score across twenty backbones. Coding-validation success reaches 69.4% versus HGM’s 64.3% at a 20.8% lower target-cost index.

Agent systems can be improved through successive revisions to their prompts, tools, and workflows. Each round proposes executable changes and then evaluates whether they improve task performance, and both consume time and computation. This raises a central question: how should an agent allocate its limited budget between exploring new revisions and verifying their benefits? Successful revisions can make later ones easier, but the evaluations that identify them are often far more expensive than proposing another edit ( Zhang et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . The difficulty is not a shortage of candidates. It is turning exploration into verified progress before time or computation runs out.

Once successors can be drafted ahead, where should we spend the budget next? A candidate that looks strong may still need several checks before it can be adopted, while a child that repairs an unhelpful parent may need only one remaining check. A scorer that only asks How good does this version look?” therefore misses the cost of making it usable. What governs the budget is not a candidate but a continuation , a sequence of further edits and checks from the current state, and the operative question becomes What verified improvement can this continuation still deliver with the remaining budget?” This quantity must be estimated before the checks that would reveal it are paid, and a wrong estimate wastes irreversible budget; this pre-verification estimate under a hard budget, not the drafting of successors, is what makes the problem hard. It shifts the scoring target from candidate quality to the marginal verified return of further editing and checking.

However, the drafting–confirmation idea cannot be transferred unchanged from tokens to agent revisions. (1) Revisions are revisable programs, not accepted prefixes. A successor may repair or build on a parent that is not yet admissible. (2) Verification consists of paid, complementary checks. External evaluations are not supplied by one target-model pass: checks have heterogeneous costs and dependencies, and several may be jointly required for adoption. (3) Progress is verified improvement under a budget. Search outcomes depend on realized gains and all incurred costs, including failed and unfinished work, rather than proposal or acceptance counts.

A Two-Level Framework for Speculative Self-Improvement. To address (1), inner loop searches extend incompletely evaluated versions but adopt only fully evaluated, admissible ones. The improver remains frozen within each search and learns from complete-search feedback between rounds.

Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS). To address (2), the Solver preserves affordable completion bundles, including individually low-value checks; the Scorer predicts verified gains from further edits and checks, net of subsequent costs; and the Policy selects the next draft or verification plan under the remaining budget.

Group Verification Optimization (GVO). To address (3), GVO uses independent complete searches from the same start as its unit of credit. Verified gains minus all search costs provide delayed credit to sampled edits and work choices, training the Drafter and Policy. Realized suffix returns and paid same-state comparisons train the Scorer.

An agent version c c comprises executable code and persistent prompts, tools, and workflows. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) revises these artifacts to support later improvement rounds. SpecRSI preserves this separation between prediction and validation, but allocates individual checks and scores further edits and checks by their eventual verified return. Accurate benefit evaluation is central to guiding RSI toward better agents. It informs which revisions and checks deserve further work, guiding the direction of improvement. Inaccurate evaluation can overlook useful revisions or waste resources on candidates that cannot be adopted. Therefore, evaluation should reflect the verified improvement that further work can deliver.

However, accurate benefit evaluation is non-trivial: a candidate’s current quality does not determine the value of continuing from it. This difficulty stems from two key challenges. 1 Benefit evaluation should reflect downstream verified improvement. Intermediate revisions may enable later gains, but establishing them requires subsequent edits and real checks. 2 Benefit evaluation should account for completion costs. Complementary checks, planning, and failed attempts consume the same limited budget; even promising gains may be unaffordable to verify. Together, these challenges create a performance–cost trade-off: a useful continuation must promise sufficient verified improvement while remaining affordable to complete. SFT uses AdamW ( 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} ; component minibatch 1; one epoch); GVO uses two frozen collection/update rounds (group 3; actor/Scorer SGD rates 10 − 3 / 5 × 10 − 4 10^{-3}/5\times 10^{-4} ; at most one joint update per complete collection). Training uses 2,048-token sequences and one H20 per scientific domain; a separate H20 serves 32,768-token inference. Other evaluated backbones use provider APIs. The repository specifies 14 versioned data pools and 42 exact member lists, model/checkpoint identities, simulator parameters, seeds, and separate training/serving software versions.
4.4 Improver Learning
RQ3: Is improvement learned by the improver, or merely retained in a stronger task agent?

Artifact controls. Improver updates raise reset/carry gains from 4.1 ± 0.18 4.1\pm 0.18 to 5.2 ± 0.21 5.2\pm 0.21 pp and from 4.8 to 6.2 pp, respectively. Original/updated improvers yield 5.7/6.9 pp from the same released artifact (Table 2 (a)), , showing gains beyond simply retaining a stronger task agent.

Repeated rounds. Updated SpecRSI reaches 21.7 pp by round 5, exceeding updated Meta by 3.9 pp (17.8 pp) and original-improver SpecRSI by 7.9 pp (13.8 pp; Table 2 (c)). All reported rounds continue to yield positive incremental gains, from 8.5 pp in round 2 to 2.1 pp in round 5.

SpecRSI’s two-level loop extends incompletely evaluated parents but adopts only complete, admissible versions. VATS allocates edits and complementary checks by predicted net verified return; GVO updates the improver from completed searches under a fixed verification contract. SpecRSI outperforms Janus in all 50 scientific backbone–task pairs and MetaRSI-v1 by 1.85–2.38 pp in four-task macro-average score across twenty backbones. Full planning achieves the highest mean verified gain and lowest total-cost index among tested planning conditions at all eight budget caps. Starting-artifact controls support gains from improver updates beyond retaining stronger task agents. Learned allocation thus turns speculation into verified agent improvement under limited budgets.

Unlike within-task reasoning search or adaptive inference compute ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Snell et al., 2025 ) , agent improvement persistently revises task solvers and their improvers. DGM, SICA, ADAS, AFlow and GEPA iteratively revise and evaluate code, workflows, or prompts ( Zhang et al., 2026a ; Robeyns et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Agrawal et al., 2026 ) ; MemEvolve co-evolves experience and memory programs, while Hyperagents and MetaRSI adapt improvement generation or scheduling ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Tan et al., 2026 ) . HGM separates lineage-metaproductivity-guided expansion from agent–task evaluation ( Wang et al., 2026b ) ; Janus co-evolves programs and proxies but retains real promotion checks ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . SpecRSI uses VATS to connect exploration to evaluation completion, jointly selecting branches and outstanding-check bundles by attainable verified improvement under the remaining budget.

Process supervision learns step evaluators; hierarchical agent RL learns long-horizon values and policies ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . GRPO estimates relative advantages for same-prompt responses ( Shao et al., 2024 ) ; DVI trains token drafters from verifier feedback; GTO targets expected tree acceptance length ( Bhansali & Heck, 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026a ) ; MAS 2 trains meta-agents with value-weighted preferences from cost-sensitive terminal outcomes ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . GVO instead credits independent complete successor searches from identical starting conditions, not responses or shared-tree leaves. Only complete admissible versions earn improvement; computation, elapsed time, failed and unfinished work remain charged. Established leave-one-out baselines and clipped updates train the drafter and work-selection policy ( Ahmadian et al., 2024 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ) ; observed-return regression trains the scorer, with paid alternative continuations supplying scorer-only labels. These updates improve later searches while the evaluator stays fixed. The contribution is this verification-grounded, cost-sensitive learning unit integrated with successor search, not a new policy-gradient estimator.

With summaries only, permitting bundles raises mean verified gain by 0.9 pp (3.2 to 4.1), compared with 1.5 pp under full-state information. At both information levels, bundles yield higher mean gain and lower total cost than the corresponding one-check controller. These fixed-information comparisons support completion-aware work scope as a contributor to VATS’s performance beyond richer inputs alone. The larger gain contrast under full state is consistent with complementarity between information and work scope; the 0.6 pp difference is descriptive rather than a significance-tested interaction. Appendix G.5 complements this empirical comparison with an exact, output-matched analysis of how permitting verification blocks can reduce dispatch cost under fixed information and explicit dispatch-cost assumptions.

The menu-cap study supports the use of a bounded planning menu in VATS (Table 3 (a); Figure S10 (a)). Increasing the cap from 8 to 32 raises mean gain from 5.2 to 6.3 percentage points and net return from 3.9 to 4.7, while reducing the missing-option percentage from 8.6% to 3.1%. Among the tested caps, 32 plans achieve the highest net return: compared with 64 plans, they yield higher net return (4.7 versus 4.5) and lower overhead (3.9 versus 5.6), while mean gain is only 0.2 percentage points lower (6.3 versus 6.5).

The menu-construction study further shows the value of completion seeds and bounded growth (Table S15 ; Figure S10 (b)). Adding completion seeds raises Final from 3.7 to 5.1, and seeded growth further raises it to 5.9. Compared with exhaustive construction, seeds plus growth achieve higher mean Final (5.9 versus 5.8) with 56.2% lower planning cost (3.9 versus 8.9), while approaching the highest Final of 6.0 obtained with the larger menu. Together, these results support VATS’s completion-seed and bounded-growth design: effective verification options can be constructed without exhaustively enumerating all combinations. Figure S10 (c) shows that Final minus Forecast decreases from − 0.1 -0.1 for singleton and seed-only menus to − 0.9 -0.9 for exhaustive construction.

Figure S11 reports the associated cost components and execution conditions. Separately, the output-matched two-check analysis in Appendix G .3.1 characterizes when dispatch savings outweigh batch-construction cost and checks made unnecessary by early failure. This trade-off motivates VATS’s state-dependent work selection: it retains feasible singleton checks and completion bundles, evaluates their downstream verified return net of cost, and replans after each executed block updates the search state. Complementary evidence in Appendix C.1 shows that, at fixed full-state information, permitting bundles raises verified gain from 4.8 to 6.3 pp while reducing the total-cost index from 63.1 to 59.2.
